_description: SwitchLingua 2.0 Stage 1 Layer 2: Group-level robust statistics for Thai-English CS (literature-based)
_note: Thai-English CS is common among urban educated youth in Bangkok and other major cities. English insertions are primarily nouns and tech/business terminology. Thai remains the strong matrix language.

Thai_social_media_CS.reference: Thaipat & Trakulkasemsuk (2020); various Thai sociolinguistic studies
Thai_social_media_CS.type: social media, spoken conversation, TV transcripts

Thai_university_CS.type: university student conversations, bilingual speech data

cmi_distribution._description: Overall CMI distribution (normalized to [0,1]), estimated from Thai-English CS literature
cmi_distribution.source: Estimated from Thai sociolinguistic studies; Gamback & Das (2014) CMI definition

by_topic._note: Topic-CMI associations based on Thai CS studies, qualitative trends

technology.note: Tech topics heavily borrow English terms, CMI high

academic.note: Academic discourse uses many English terms

food.note: Food topics almost entirely Thai except foreign cuisine names

entertainment.note: Entertainment topics moderate mixing due to English media

switch_type_distribution._description: Switch type distribution (robust statistics, based on Thai CS literature)

intra_sentential.note: Intra-sentential switching dominant, primarily noun/NP insertion

switch_position_distribution.source: Thai CS studies; Thai SVO structure similar to English facilitates NP switching

NP_boundary.note: Noun phrase position most common, consistent with insertion model. Thai SVO order facilitates English NP insertion

VP_boundary.note: Verb phrase position less common than NP

CP_boundary.note: Clause/sentence boundary, corresponds to alternation pattern

discourse_marker.note: Discourse marker position (okay, right, so, นะ, อะ, etc.)

high_frequency_L2_elements._description: High frequency English insertions in Thai-English CS
high_frequency_L2_elements.source: Thai CS literature + Thai social media observations
L2_fixed_expressions_top30: at the end of the day

archetype_distribution_estimate._description: Estimated proportion of each archetype in real Thai-English CS data
archetype_distribution_estimate._method: Based on CMI distribution and switch type patterns from Thai CS literature

ARC_01_insertional.reasoning: CMI < 0.25 with mostly intra-sentential switching. Most common pattern among Thai speakers — English nouns inserted into Thai frame

ARC_02_alternational.reasoning: CMI 0.25-0.45 with higher inter-sentential proportion. Common among internationally educated Thai speakers

ARC_03_dense_mixer.reasoning: CMI > 0.45, frequent switching. Less common, mainly international school graduates and long-term overseas returnees

ARC_04_pragmatic.reasoning: Variable CMI with pragmatically motivated switching. Common in professional and media contexts

ARC_05_reluctant.reasoning: CMI < 0.10, Thai-only with minimal English. Common among older or less English-educated speakers

ARC_06_accommodation.reasoning: CMI varies significantly across conversations based on interlocutor

ARC_07_backflag.reasoning: English-dominant with Thai markers. Rare, mainly Thai diaspora or long-term overseas residents

validation_notes.confidence: Moderate — based on literature trends and sociolinguistic observations rather than large-scale corpus statistics
limitations: No single large-scale Thai-English CS corpus comparable to SEAME exists
Thai social media CS data is abundant but not systematically annotated
Topic-CMI associations are qualitative trends, not precise values
Archetype distribution estimates are rough approximations
next_steps: Compile Thai-English CS corpus from Thai social media (Twitter, Pantip, LINE)
Annotate Thai-English CS in university student conversations
Validate CMI distribution against annotated data
Refine archetype proportions with speaker-level analysis
